newsitem.title: GERMANY: FEATURE - Germany sells off history in EMU drive.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Germany sells off history in EMU drive.

text.p: Nothing is sacred, it seems, in Germany's drive to sell off state property, reduce its debts and make the grade for Europe's single currency.

Germany's privatisation drive has claimed once-entrenched monopolies like Deutsche Telekom and Lufthansa. The country's strategic oil reserves are up for sale. Some politicians even want to sell off emergency stocks of peas, hoarded to feed survivors of a possible nuclear attack.

Now the government has put its exclusive Petersberg hotel near Bonn on the market, saying it will have no use for it as a residence for visiting heads of state after Berlin takes over as reunified Germany's political capital in 1999.

Perched like a hilltop monastery above the Rhine valley "the Petersberg" offers an apparently enticing prospect for investors, with 92 rooms, two restaurants and 110 hectares (271.8 acres) of parkland in which an 18th century chapel stands.
All that, along with room rates of up to 1,200 marks ($700) a night, could could tempt an upmarket hotel chain as a buyer.
LOCALS OPPOSE SALE
But locals say it would be a travesty if the Petersberg, built in 1914 on an ancient pilgrimage site, ends up being turned into a casino -- as one plan envisages.
"It's wrong to sell the Petersberg because of its history, which is so closely tied to the that of the Federal Republic," local historian Winfried Giesing told Reuters.
Indeed, the sale will not just end a roll-call of guests which began in 1955 with the Shah of Iran and includes King Hussein of Jordan and Britain's Queen Elizabeth II.

It will also draw the line under an era of turbulent history in which the hotel was a silent witness to Nazi leader Adolf Hitler's grab for land in central Europe, and the birth of a new German state from the devastation of World War Two.

It was here, in September 1938, that British prime minister Neville Chamberlain stayed during one of his missions to try to persuade Hitler not to send troops into Czechoslovakia's German-speaking Sudetenland.
The following month, at the Munich summit, Chamberlain won a pledge from Hitler not to occupy the region.
Proclaiming "peace in our time" from the window of Number 10, Downing Street, the British premier believed his shuttle diplomacy had contained Hitler's ambitions.
But he had overestimated his own powers of persuasion.
Hitler's subsequent treachery discredited London's policy of appeasement and ensured that the Nazi invasion of Poland the following summer would lead to all-out war.
ADENAUER'S FAUX PAS
The Petersberg's exclusive clique of guests vanished during the war and the hotel was closed and suffered artillery damage.
In 1945 it was taken over by the western Allies, who used it as a joint high commission to rule what was to become the German Federal Republic.

By 1949, the U.S., France and Britain were ready to restore limited self-government and it was here at the Petersberg that West Germany's first Chancellor, Konrad Adenauer, presented his inaugural cabinet of ministers.

In a famous breach of etiquette, Adenauer stepped onto a hand-woven rug reserved for the high commissioners, signalling the confidence with which the wily chancellor later led his country's post-war economic miracle.
From the mid-1950s the government in Bonn, Adenauer's chosen capital, hosted a stream of leaders at the Petersberg, and Soviet president Leonid Brezhnev caused a stir when he came to stay in 1973.
Chancellor Willy Brandt gave Brezhnev a new Mercedes coupe, which the Soviet president promptly crashed in a ditch during a test drive on the Petersberg's winding approach road.

Early reports that Brezhnev might have been badly injured proved unfounded, and it turned out that he had just put a hole in the Mercedes' oil sump. The red-faced Kremlin chief was given a replacement car to take home to Moscow.
The roll-call of the famous goes on -- two-time Formula One motor racing world champion Michael Schumacher held his wedding reception here a couple of years ago.
NOT SO EASY TO SELL

But, as hotel manager Richard Freymann told Reuters in an interview, anyone wanting to buy the Petersberg will not be investing in one of those cheap-to-run, boxy business hotels that dominate cities today.

The costs of maintaining its extensive grounds, as well as the right reserved by the government to throw out guests to make room for official visitors means the hotel needs an annual subsidy of three million marks to get by.

And calls by the Rhine resort town of Koenigswinter to keep public access to the woodland around the Petersberg -- which is part of a public park -- rule out a purchase by a reclusive business magnate or rock star.
"You simply could not sell the Petersberg to someone like Michael Jackson," Freymann said.
The Foreign Ministry, which owns the Petersberg, has hired merchant bank M.M. Warburg to manage the hotel's sale, and 30 bidders are in the running, a spokeswoman said.
Bankers at Warburg declined to comment in detail, but said both wealthy individuals and hotel groups were in the running.
And, if press reports are to be believed, the Petersberg -- and a piece of German history -- could go to the highest bidder for around 200 million marks ($110 million).
